newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Latin Americans tire of waiting for economic benefits.
newsitem.headline: Latin Americans tire of waiting for economic benefits.

text.p: Latin Americans, weary of waiting for the benefits of free market reforms, are showing their impatience in renewed social unrest, rebel violence and electoral defeats of the kind dealt to Mexico's ruling party.
Symptoms of "reform fatigue" have surfaced in many nations that abandoned protectionism a decade ago in favour of policies making them more competitive and attractive to investment.
Leaders have succeeded best at vanquishing hyperinflation, but fostered only modest economic growth, in most cases higher unemployment and little or no progress on poverty.

"An increasing number of people are disillusioned, and there is a slowly growing sense of reform scepticism," Sebastian Edwards, a former World Bank chief economist for Latin America, wrote in Foreign Affairs magazine recently.
"Is it realistic to ask the public to continue to back politicians who request patience while they are unable to deliver improved economic conditions?"

On Sunday, Mexico's opposition delivered the ruling party its worst drubbing in seven decades by wresting control of the lower house of Congress and the mayoralty of Mexico City. The new mayor, leftist Cuauhtemoc Cardenas, promised to push "for a more social face to economic policy."
Focus on social issues in Latin America will remain high with presidential contests scheduled for Venezuela and Brazil next year, Argentina in 1999 and Mexico and Peru in 2000.

The greatest victory has been over hyperinflation. Prices across the region are expected to rise an average of only 12 percent this year. Real economic growth was an average 3.4 percent a year from 1991-1996 after 2.2 percent in 1985-90.
But more Latin Americans are out of work. In at least 10 countries, including the big economies of Mexico, Brazil and Argentina, unemployment was higher in 1996 than 1991.
In the four large nations with available data - Argentina, Brazil, Mexico and Peru - the percentage of poor people was up slightly in 1990s from the 1980s, according to the World Bank.
An opinion poll by Chile's Latinobarometro shows 70 percent of Latin Americans do not perceive the gains brought by economic growth and believe poverty has risen.

Ricardo Hausmann, chief economist for the Inter-American Development Bank, says reforms have "even exacerbated existing social problems. The increasing fatigue of many social groups requires that governments focus on social problems."
The resurgence of guerrilla movements in Colombia, Mexico and Peru can at least in part be attributed to poverty there. So can a crime wave in most major Latin American cities.
Mexican reforms cut inflation from 160 percent in 1987 to 10 percent in 1993, but poverty has quadrupled to 51 percent since 1984.

In Peru, where Marxist guerrillas held hostages at the Japanese embassy for four months this year, Fujimori vows to halve extreme poverty, gripping 19 percent of the population, by 2000. But private data shows total poverty at 75 percent.

Argentina's Peronist government, hit by scores of protests over 17.3 percent unemployment on the eve of October congressional elections, is considering several job creation projects that would involve billions of dollars in spending.

A 1994 Brazil stabilisation plan cut inflation from 5,000 percent to single digit levels and officials say they reduced poverty to 25 percent from 33 percent since. While President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's support has fallen, he is still twice as popular as leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

Chile, the first to systematically introduce reforms, is the example. Real wages fell eight percent between 1970 and 1989. Since then they have risen 3.9 percent. Poverty has dropped from 45.1 percent in 1987 to 32.2 percent last year.
Analysts say years of reforms are still needed to boost competitiveness and infrastructure and loosen labour laws.
The threat now is that popular demand for respite from austerity will bring reversals in the reform process.

"Most political leaders realise that the reform process must intensify in order to build truly robust economies," said Edwards. "It is unclear, however, whether more rapid reform will be politically feasible."
